messages.subject: Implications of non-independence between sessions in Multi-session models
messages.subject_clean: Implications of non-independence between sessions in Multi-session models
messages.body_plain:
Hello Murray and everyone,

When using multi-session models to estimate density for multiple years, but on species where there is considerable overlap in individuals between years (i.e., sessions are not independent) - what are the main caveats?

Murray mentions in the multi-session documentation that the density estimate errors will be too narrow for each year.

Wouldn't one expect other issues? Would it also impact estimates of detection covariates, density covariates, etc? Would IC based model selection be biased?

I'm finding several papers that published density trends for large carnivores that don't even mention this concern.

Any insights and pointers would be much appreciated.

Best,

Mirjam

messages.subject: Re: Implications of non-independence between sessions in Multi-session models
messages.subject_clean: Implications of non-independence between sessions in Multi-session models
messages.body_plain:
Hi Mirjam

Interesting. I think the problem can be overstated, but it is there, and could use some serious attention (have you tried simulation?). Repeated sampling of the same AC while assuming independence results in overdispersion. Overdispersion inflates true sampling variance and reduces CI coverage, but has negligible effect on estimates themselves (does not cause bias). IC-based model selection is affected in principle, but should we really be taking that so seriously anyway?

Thinking aloud... The overdispersion we are talking about affects the 'n' component of the sampling variance of density (number of individuals detected), not the 'a' component (detection). Sampling the same population over and over is equivalent to sampling a highly clustered population. At worst (no turnover, no movement between sessions, high detection rate, low variance in a-hat), the true 'n' variance component might be inflated by the number of sessions (#AC per cluster).

Other approaches: try an open model (not my preferred solution because there are big overheads and the open model itself may be wrong); join multi-session data as single session (obvious risk of bias from turnover within duration of study, but maybe informative on variance).

Murray

messages.subject: Re: Implications of non-independence between sessions in Multi-session models
messages.subject_clean: Implications of non-independence between sessions in Multi-session models
messages.body_plain:
Well, I really don't like open models for density estimation, so expect some push back if I get to review your paper! The problem of temporal overdispersion does not arise if you use Horvitz-Thompson (derived) density estimates.That is a nice out: you get to fit a pooled (multi-year) model for estimating detection parameters, and AIC comparisons of such models are unaffected by temporal overdispersion. Annual CI for density are based on the number detected in each year, rather than the inflated number (summed over years). Of course this does not allow any model for density, specifically a trend model, which may be the whole point of the analysis.
Murray

messages.subject: Potential Bug with site-level variation
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm running a model with data from 10 different sites across 2 years, where density is modeled as a function of both spatial covariates and a site-level effect. The models run great and are able to get an estimate for the betas. However, region.N and predictD give the error: "Error in mat %*% betaD : non-conformable arguments"

Using the source code on Github, I've tracked down the error. It comes  from the model.matrix() or general.model.matrix() functions or right around there. The model gives the density formula as ~opnearl_wg84 + site. General.model.matrix() interprets this as 3 betas - the intercept, the beta for opnearl_wg84 and a beta for site, but it actually needs to be interpreted as a factor and turn into 11 betas (intercept/reference level, opnearl_wg84 and 9 sites) so that it matches the dimensions of betaD. Trying to get around this by expanding out the factor levels into binary variables in the mask doesn't help, since region.N filters out all covariates that aren't relevant, and it doesn't recognize "siteSITE1" or "siteSITE2" as connected to the "site" covariate used in density estimation.

I've created a workaround for my very specific problem, but just wanted to let everyone know that this might come up in the future.

-Heather

messages.body_plain:
Interesting. Horvitz-Thompson estimates wouldn't allow for an inhomogeneous density model, though, either, right? Which is the whole point of the analysis, and necessary -  our study area is too large and too inhomogeneous to not use density models when estimating density. We're not as much interested in temporal trends, as the study didn't last long enough to detect temp trends unless they're incredibly drastic.

So what do you suggest researchers do who cannot ignore spatial effects on density in their final models, but still need to sample large areas, usually over several years (to answer other questions, too - can't just count them) to get density estimates because their study species are wide ranging and also long lived but hard to detect?

Best,
Mirjam

messages.subject: Basic openCR questions about primary and secondary sessions
messages.subject_clean: Basic openCR questions about primary and secondary sessions
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am hoping to get some advice as I am just starting a mark recapture analysis, using openCR to estimate density. I have read lots of the vignettes and guides but before I get too deep into the models I'd like some basic help with how to structure the data.

I have data from 15 years of trapping a species at a single site. The site was divided into three sections and each year the sections were trapped 4 times (e.g. all sections trapped once in Jan, once in April, July and October; the exact dates changed each year but stuck to the seasons). The areas are not distinct in terms of home ranges - the species' home ranges are likely to overlap between different sections.

I've organised the data so the years are the primary sessions with each trapping event being a secondary session (15 primary sessions (years), 12 secondary sessions per year). However, the population isn't closed between the trapping events, so should the trapping events (12 a year) be the primary sessions instead, each with one secondary session? That would be 180 primary (and secondary) sessions. Or alternatively, should the months be the primary sessions (4 a year) each with 3 secondary sessions (representing the three areas of the site trapped in sequence in that month) - but I can't assume closure between the secondary sessions in this case.

Also, because the three areas of the site were trapped in sequence,  the number/position of traps changed with each trapping session (i.e. we started with the traps in section 1, then moved to section 2, then 3, each month). Would that mean I'd need a different detector file/mask for each primary session, or can you specify which traps were used with a 'usage' argument?

I am interested in looking at the change in density over time but most interested in the most recent density estimate. Am I overcomplicating it? Should I just look at the most recent years of data?

Thanks so much,

Sarah

messages.subject: Re: Basic openCR questions about primary and secondary sessions
messages.subject_clean: Basic openCR questions about primary and secondary sessions
messages.body_plain:
I would have thought each month was a primary session (allowing turnover between primary sessions, presumably modelled with a 'season' covariate). It seems you have no opportunity for within-month recaptures, except maybe between sections. Did you get within-month movement between sections? If not then you could save some trouble by treating sampling within each month as synchronous across sections. Otherwise there will be three sequential secondary sessions in each month, and you will need to identify the active section on each with the usage attribute. In any case, the same mask can be used for all (it doesn't hurt if it's larger than needed for a particular section).

It seems the data don't lend themselves to closed population analysis, so I won't push that. I suggest starting with just annual samples (e.g., Jan in each year), assuming you have a long-lived species.

Murray

messages.subject: Re: Potential Bug with site-level variation
messages.body_plain:
Hi Heather
Can you please provide more code and context? I do not see a problem with this fake example (arbitrarily generating 'sites' from the grids of possumCH).
Murray

library(secr)
grid <- substring(rownames(traps(possumCH)), 1,2)
covariates(possummask)$grid <- factor(grid[nearesttrap(possummask, traps(possumCH))])

plot(possummask, cov='grid')
plot(traps(possumCH), add=T)

fit <- secr.fit(possumCH, mask = possummask, D ~ x + y + grid)
coef(fit)
#                 beta    SE.beta        lcl        ucl
# D         0.30025341 0.26994201 -0.2288232  0.8293300
# D.x       0.22512618 0.48666096 -0.7287118  1.1789641
# D.y       0.04205227 0.37118572 -0.6854584  0.7695629
# D.gridG2 -0.09976331 0.56668561 -1.2104467  1.0109201
# D.gridG3  0.17377280 0.63202951 -1.0649823  1.4125279
# D.gridG4  0.14544947 0.78357986 -1.3903388  1.6812378
# D.gridG5  0.67232770 0.72558724 -0.7497972  2.0944526
# g0       -1.43600678 0.14054143 -1.7114629 -1.1605506
# sigma     3.94227490 0.04967478  3.8449141  4.0396357

masklist <- split(possummask, covariates(possummask)$grid)
lapply(masklist, region.N, object = fit)

plot(predictDsurface(fit))
plot(traps(possumCH), add=T)

>
> I've created a workaround for my very specific problem, but just wanted to let everyone know that this might come up in the future.
>
> -Heather

messages.body_plain:
Heather

Thanks for sending your data offline. I have revised my earlier diagnosis [now deleted] as follows.

Your ‘site’ predictor is a character mask covariate. You provide different masks for each year, and exclude from the first mask two sites not sampled in that year. As a result, when the session-specific site covariate is converted internally from character to factor, factor levels do not match across years, and the beta parameters for the site covariate in the first year do not match those in the second year.

The solution is to apply shareFactorLevels() to the multi-session mask _before_ fitting the model (and there’s really no need for a multi-session mask). Applying this retrospectively, as I suggested earlier, gives the _wrong_ answer because it mismatches sites and coefficients. Your workaround is also wrong for the same reason.

Why is the problem not flagged by secr.fit()? The verify function applied to a multi-session mask does throw a warning and suggest using shareFactorLevels(), but within secr.fit() verify is mistakenly applied only to each separate session-specific mask, and therefore fails to find the inconsistency.

Murray

messages.subject: Re: Potential Bug with site-level variation
messages.body_plain:
I'm glad that worked. It is not necessary for all factor levels to be represented in every session, only that a factor covariate has a set of levels that is constant across sessions, so that there is a consistent relationship between levels and beta parameters (coefficients). As I understand it, the scenario you describe is really just a variation on your original one, where not all levels of 'site' were sampled in the first year (or not all vegetation classes appear in each year).
Murray
